title: Emotions Beat Facts in Climate Campaigns — Study
paragraphs: Climate campaigns that appeal to people's emotions are much more effective than those that rely on facts, according to a new review of research.

A research team at the University of Geneva wanted to find out what types of campaign message are most likely to motivate people to take action against climate change and to support ambitious climate policies.
The researchers analyzed the findings of 71 previous studies that looked at the impact of different climate communication strategies.

The team reviewed 15 different strategies within the studies, including methods such as presenting facts and scientific evidence, discussing the economic or health consequences of climate change, or deliberately evoking an emotional response.

The researchers found that almost all of the strategies consistently increased people's climate-related intentions and actions, and their support for climate policies. Only strategies that called on people's sense of individual or collective responsibility were found to be ineffective — in fact they could even trigger a negative reaction.

However, strategies designed to evoke an emotional response were much more effective than just presenting facts and evidence. In particular, storytelling or inspiring a sense of awe at the beauty of nature produced the best results.
Strategies that appealed to people's sense of ethical or religious duty were also found to be more effective. And in general, messages that included images were more effective than those that didn't.
One of the researchers, Tobias Brosch, said the fact that almost all the strategies had a positive effect was encouraging.

However, what was particularly encouraging, he added, was that most of the studies measured the effects of messages that were given only once, but previous research has shown that such messages have even more impact when they are repeated.
"At a time when the scientific evidence is well established and the challenge is to turn knowledge into action, there is considerable scope to improve climate communication," Brosch said.
